# Introduction

Forest research teams often have several sources of environmental information for the same plot. Elevation may come from a ground survey or a digital elevation model. Soil measurements may be stored as a table of sampling locations, while canopy height or disturbance intensity may arrive as raster files. These sources can describe different years, spatial resolutions and areas of coverage. This tutorial shows how to put those sources into a common spatial frame. It also shows how to extract environmental information at different scales:

-   specific points, e.g. tree locations;
-   buffers around specific points;
-   quadrats;
-   polygons of arbitrary shape.

The example data used here combines real elevation and soil data for the 50-ha Barro Colorado Island (BCI) plot in Panama. Terrain layers come from the `derive_topography()` workflow applied to elevational data. Soil layers are prepared independently. Native raster grids are retained for extraction, and an additional example shows how to create a common grid when an analysis needs one. Habitat classification and categorical extraction are covered separately. All inputs are in `data_examples/` at the repository root. See its [dataset notes](../../data_examples/README.md) for provenance.

-   **`census1.txt`** and **`census2.txt`** contain the first two BCI tree censuses, nominally 1982 and 1985. They are historical census exports already included in fgeo2. Census 1 measurements span 1981--1983. Credit goes to the BCI census team, including Stephen P. Hubbell, Robin B. Foster, Richard Condit and collaborators, and Smithsonian/ForestGEO.
-   **`bci-elevation.csv`** contains 20,301 elevation grid locations, with columns `x`, `y` and `z` in metres. Its numerical contents match `BCIelev.tsv` in the Condit et al. archive, released under CC0. Positions run from 0 to 1,000 m in x and 0 to 500 m in y, at 5 m intervals. These are input grid locations, rather than raster-cell boundaries.
-   **`bci-soils-wolf-2015.csv`** is the complete soil dataset of Wolf et al. (2015), [Geospatial observations on tropical forest surface soil chemistry](#0). It includes 625 sampled locations, all soil variables and both local and UTM coordinates. The [publisher's dataset deposit](#0) is CC0. P and Ca illustrate the main workflow, while all measurements remain available for other analyses.

# Setup and loading

Run from the repository root or this tutorial's folder. When working elsewhere, replace `path.to.fgeo2` with the full path to your local repository. Output files go to a temporary folder by default.

```{r}
#| label: setup-environment
#| results: hide
#| message: false

# install.packages(c("terra", "sf", "interp", "exactextractr"))
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(exactextractr)

path.to.fgeo2 = if(file.exists("../../fgeo2.Rproj")) "../.." else "."
# path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"
input.dir = file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "data_examples")
output.dir = file.path(tempdir(), "fgeo2-environment")
dir.create(output.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-variables.R"))
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/quadrats.R"))

# Shared options. Interpolation choices are described below.
plot.extent = c(0, 1000, 0, 500)  # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax
terrain.resolution = 5
soil.resolution = 20
buffer.radius = 15
set.seed(123)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
```

## Census records and stable identifiers

Read tags and identifiers as character strings, preserving leading zeros. The stem identifier is unique within each supplied census. A combined census--stem key distinguishes repeated observations of the same stem. Several stems can belong to one tree.

```{r}
#| label: load-censuses

id.columns <- c(TreeID = "character",
                StemID = "character",
                Tag = "character",
                StemTag = "character",
                Quadrat = "character")

census1 <- read.delim(file.path(input.dir, "census1.txt"),
                      colClasses = id.columns, check.names = FALSE)

census2 <- read.delim(file.path(input.dir, "census2.txt"),
                      colClasses = id.columns, check.names = FALSE)

trees <- rbind(census1, census2)
trees$point_id <- paste(trees$Census, trees$StemID, sep = "_")
stopifnot(!anyNA(trees$point_id), !anyDuplicated(trees$point_id))

```

## Elevation and soil tables

Keep the complete input tables. Variable selection takes place when preparing layers for a particular analysis. The original soil file contains a space before the `utm_n` column name, which is removed on import here. Its [metadata](https://esapubs.org/archive/ecol/E096/204/metadata.php) describes methods, units, missing values and detection limits.

```{r}
#| label: load-environment

xyz <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, "bci-elevation.csv"))
soils <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, "bci-soils-wolf-2015.csv"),
                  check.names = FALSE)

names(soils) <- trimws(names(soils))
stopifnot(nrow(xyz) == 20301L, nrow(soils) == 625L,
          !anyDuplicated(xyz[c("x", "y")]), !anyDuplicated(soils$uid))

head(soils[c("uid", "gx", "gy", "M3P", "M3Ca")])
```

# Prepare raster layers

## Coordinate congruence

Census `PX, PY`, Wolf's soil `gx, gy` and elevation `x, y` use the same local plot coordinates, in metres. Here x increases eastward from the western edge and y increases northward from the southern edge. We use `"local"` throughout; check that any additional plot data share this origin, axis directions and units.

External sources such as remote-sensing products need CRS alignment and standard GIS checks before use (`sf::st_transform()` or `terra::project()`, as appropriate). Assigning a CRS label alone does not align coordinates.

## Terrain from the elevation grid

The call uses default linear interpolation and selects variables available without WhiteboxTools. Elevation is returned automatically. This is an application of the completed [terrain workflow](derive-topographical-variables.qmd). TPI describes relative topographic position at the selected neighbourhood scale. Northness and eastness are relative to the local plot-grid axes here.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-terrain

terrain <- derive_topography(
	xyz = xyz,
	variables = c("slope", "tpi", "northness", "eastness"),
	resolution = terrain.resolution,
	extent = plot.extent,
	crs = "local",
	position.radius = 20
)

names(terrain)
```

## Soil measurements to continuous layers

The soil coordinates are sampling locations. They form an approximately 28 m sampling design with small positional offsets. For this tutorial example, inverse-distance weighting estimates P and Ca on a 20 m grid. A 60 m search radius, up to 12 neighbours, at least 3 observations and power 2 are explicit example settings. The resulting cells describe interpolated estimates, not true measurement accuracy or uniform density of information. But this is standard practice, so in general you don't have to worry about this if data comes from a reasonable representative survey.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-soil

soil.template <- rast(xmin = 0, xmax = 1000, ymin = 0, ymax = 500,
                       resolution = soil.resolution, crs = "local")
soil.variables <- c("M3P", "M3Ca")
soil.layers <- vector("list", length(soil.variables))

for(i in seq_along(soil.variables))
{
	variable <- soil.variables[i]
	keep <- is.finite(soils$gx) & is.finite(soils$gy) & is.finite(soils[[variable]])
	measurements <- as.matrix(soils[keep, c("gx", "gy", variable)])
	soil.layers[[i]] <- interpIDW(soil.template, measurements,
	                              radius = 60, power = 2,
	                              minPoints = 3, maxPoints = 12)

	# Avoid extending these predictions beyond the sampling locations' hull.
	locations <- vect(soils[keep, ], geom = c("gx", "gy"), crs = "local")
	soil.layers[[i]] <- mask(soil.layers[[i]], convHull(locations), touches = FALSE)
}

soil <- rast(soil.layers)
names(soil) <- c("soil_P_mgkg", "soil_Ca_mgkg")
units(soil) <- c("mg/kg", "mg/kg")
```

For a table that already describes a complete regular grid of **cell centres**, conversion can be much shorter. Cell-centre positions and cell boundaries must be distinguished to avoid a half-cell shift.

```{r}
#| label: regular-table-template
#| eval: false

# Columns x and y are centres of cells in a known regular grid.
# Additional columns become separate raster layers.
regular.layers <- rast(my.table[c("x", "y", "soil_P", "soil_Ca")],
                        type = "xyz", crs = "local")
```

If environmental values are already recorded for the supplied quadrats, a direct ID join may be sufficient. Raster conversion is useful when the subsequent analysis actually needs a surface.

## Optional soil principal components

Soil surveys often contain many correlated variables, and soils are usually described in terms of "soil axes". This optional example standardizes the measurement columns and fits PCA to complete rows. It excludes identifiers and coordinates, and preserves row alignment when storing scores.

```{r}
#| label: soil-pca
#| eval: false

coordinate.columns <- c("uid", "qid", "gx", "gy", "utm_e", "utm_n")
soil.columns <- setdiff(names(soils), c(coordinate.columns, "soil_PC1"))
keep <- complete.cases(soils[soil.columns])
soil.pca <- prcomp(soils[keep, soil.columns], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
soils$soil_PC1 <- NA_real_
soils$soil_PC1[keep] <- soil.pca$x[, 1]
summary(soil.pca)

# To map PC1, apply the soil-interpolation block to soil_PC1.
# Retain soil.pca itself to inspect loadings and reproduce the scores.
```

# Combine sources and check their grids

## Retain native grids

A named list can hold the terrain and soil rasters together while preserving each grid. Sources with compatible grids can already be combined into a multilayer `SpatRaster`. Extraction below works through this list and joins the results by target identity.

```{r}
#| label: native-grids

environment <- list(terrain = terrain, soil = soil)

str(environment)
str(environment$terrain)
dim(environment$terrain)
str(environment$soil)
dim(environment$soil)

compareGeom(terrain, soil, stopOnError = FALSE)
```

Missing terrain neighbourhoods and the soil sampling hull create different valid footprints, even though both raster extents describe the full plot. Each variable therefore needs its own coverage calculation.

## Create a common grid when needed

For cell-wise calculations, use one chosen template. Here both sources have the same extent, origin and CRS, and 20 m is an integer multiple of 5 m. Aggregating groups of 4 × 4 terrain cells produces a compatible grid. With compatible grids, adding variables is simply `c()`.

```{r}
#| label: common-grid

terrain20 <- aggregate(terrain, fact = 4, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(compareGeom(terrain20, soil))
common.grid <- c(terrain20, soil)
names(common.grid)
```

These are means of the fine-resolution terrain variables. Calculating slope or TPI afresh from a coarser DEM would define a different quantity. `na.rm = TRUE` also permits partially observed aggregate cells, so retain native layers for the coverage-aware extraction below.

For other situations, choose the operation according to the actual mismatch.

| Situation                                  | Operation and interpretation                                                                        |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Same grid, additional variables            | `c()` adds layers after `compareGeom()` checks.                                                     |
| Aligned fine cells to larger cells         | `aggregate()` summarizes groups of cells.                                                           |
| Same CRS, different grid origin or spacing | `resample()` transfers values to an explicit template. Choose a method appropriate to the variable. |
| Adjacent tiles of one variable             | `merge()` or `mosaic()` combines spatial tiles.                                                     |

For continuous point-like surfaces, bilinear resampling is a possible interpolation choice. For larger output cells covering several input cells, a mean may be appropriate. A value representing a block mean has a different meaning from a measurement at its centre. Smoothing changes the environmental surface and should have a stated analytical purpose. Finer output cells retain the information limits of the original source.

```{r}
#| label: resampling-template
#| eval: false

# Same known CRS, but grids that do not align.
soil.on.terrain.grid <- resample(soil, terrain[[1]], method = "bilinear")
# A coarser output template may instead call for method = "mean".
```

# Extract at point (tree) coordinates

This example uses three tree species. The extraction itself works on points: it has no species-specific requirements and can be applied to all supplied records.

```{r}
#| label: choose-tree-targets
spp <- c("beilpe", "virosu", "elaeol")
use <- which(trees$Mnemonic %in% spp & trees$Status == "alive")
targets <- trees[use, c("point_id", "Census", "StemID", "Mnemonic", "PX", "PY")]

rownames(targets) <- NULL
table(targets$Census, targets$Mnemonic)
```

The `terra::extract()` function crosses layers with sampling points; `method = "simple"` returns the value of the cell containing each point. Optional bilinear sampling estimates a value from nearby cell centres and changes the sampling operation.

Initialize the complete output before extracting rows with finite coordinates. The `ID` returned by terra refers to row positions in the supplied point geometry, so map it back through `point.i`. Duplicate coordinates are allowed for different records. Missing coordinates, outside points and missing cells all retain their input rows.

```{r}
#| label: sample-points

point.env <- targets
point.i <- which(is.finite(targets$PX) & is.finite(targets$PY))
points <- NULL
if(length(point.i))
	points <- vect(targets[point.i, ], geom = c("PX", "PY"), crs = "local")

for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	for(variable in names(layers)) point.env[[variable]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(targets))
	point.env[[paste0(source, "_cell")]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(targets))

	if(!length(point.i)) next
	extracted <- terra::extract(layers, points, method = "simple", cells = TRUE)
	original.i <- point.i[extracted$ID]
	point.env[original.i, names(layers)] <- extracted[, names(layers), drop = FALSE]
	point.env[original.i, paste0(source, "_cell")] <- extracted$cell
}

stopifnot(identical(point.env$point_id, targets$point_id))

# check output
head(point.env[c("point_id", "Mnemonic", "elevation_m", "soil_P_mgkg")])

# simple summary to group the extracted values by species. 
aggregate(point.env[c("elevation_m", "soil_P_mgkg", "soil_Ca_mgkg")],
          by = list(point.env$Mnemonic), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Extract from buffers

All polygon-based extractions work in the same way. The tutorial separates buffers, quadrats and arbitrary polygons for didactic purposes; only the construction of the targets and their identifiers changes.

## Construct buffers

The radius is in metres because these are local metre coordinates. Buffers can overlap and cross the plot boundary. Each remains a separate target with its original point ID. Missing-coordinate records have no buffer geometry, but keep their requested output rows.

```{r}
#| label: point-buffers

point.sf <- st_sf(point_id = character(),
                  geometry = st_sfc(crs = st_crs(crs(terrain))))

if(length(point.i))
	point.sf <- st_as_sf(targets[point.i, ], coords = c("PX", "PY"),
	                     crs = st_crs(crs(terrain)))

buffers <- st_buffer(point.sf, dist = buffer.radius)
buffer.area <- as.numeric(st_area(buffers))
```

## Extract environmental summaries

An area mean weights each cell by its overlap with the target. Valid coverage is their overlap area divided by the full target area. Coverage of 0.7 means that 30% of the target contributes no values, because of missing cells or an area beyond the raster. Calculate it separately for each variable, on that layer's native grid. The same definitions apply to the quadrats and arbitrary polygons below.

### Method 1 with terra::extract()

With `exact = TRUE` and `fun = mean`, terra weights values by overlap fractions. Extracting `!is.na(layers)` with `fun = sum` gives the sum of valid fractions. Multiplying by cell area and dividing by target area gives coverage. As for points, terra's `ID` refers to geometry row positions; `point.i` restores the complete target table.

```{r}
#| label: terra-buffer-means

buffer.terra <- targets
for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	
	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		buffer.terra[[paste0("mean.", variable)]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(targets))
		buffer.terra[[paste0("coverage.", variable)]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(targets))
	}
	
	if(!length(point.i)) next
	
	means <- terra::extract(layers, vect(buffers), exact = TRUE, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
	counts <- terra::extract(!is.na(layers), vect(buffers), exact = TRUE, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)
	i <- match(seq_along(point.i), means$ID)
	j <- match(seq_along(point.i), counts$ID)

	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		value <- means[[variable]][i]
		value[is.nan(value)] <- NA_real_
		coverage <- counts[[variable]][j] * prod(res(layers)) / buffer.area
		coverage[is.na(coverage)] <- 0
		buffer.terra[point.i, paste0("mean.", variable)] <- value
		buffer.terra[point.i, paste0("coverage.", variable)] <- pmin(1, pmax(0, coverage))
	}
	
}
```

Terra's direct exact summaries support mean, sum, min, max and class tables. Other statistics can use raw values and fractions. For example, this would calculate standard deviation of soil P in the first buffer:

```{r}
#| label: terra-custom-summary

spatial.sd <- NA_real_
if(nrow(buffers))
{
	overlap <- terra::extract(soil[["soil_P_mgkg"]], vect(buffers[1, ]), exact = TRUE)
	keep <- is.finite(overlap$soil_P_mgkg) & is.finite(overlap$fraction) & overlap$fraction > 0
	values <- overlap$soil_P_mgkg[keep]
	weights <- overlap$fraction[keep]
	if(length(values))
	{
		average <- weighted.mean(values, weights)
		spatial.sd <- sqrt(weighted.mean((values - average)^2, weights))
	}
}
spatial.sd
```

### Method 2 with exactextractr::exact_extract()

The `exactextract()` function in the R package `exactextractr` accepts the same `SpatRaster` layers and `sf` polygons. Here it supplies overlap-weighted means, medians and population SDs. Its `count` is the sum of valid cell fractions, used to calculate coverage. `append_cols` preserves the point identifier for joining the results back.

```{r}
#| label: exactextractr-buffer-summaries

buffer.env <- targets
for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	
	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		for(statistic in c("mean", "median", "stdev", "count", "coverage"))
			buffer.env[[paste(statistic, variable, sep = ".")]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(targets))
	}
	
	if(!length(point.i)) next
	
	extracted <- exact_extract(layers, buffers,
		fun = c("mean", "median", "stdev", "count"),
		append_cols = "point_id", full_colnames = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		coverage <- extracted[[paste0("count.", variable)]] * prod(res(layers)) / buffer.area
		coverage[is.na(coverage)] <- 0
		extracted[[paste0("coverage.", variable)]] <- pmin(1, pmax(0, coverage))
	}
	
	original.i <- match(extracted$point_id, targets$point_id)
	
	for(column in setdiff(names(extracted), "point_id"))
	{
		extracted[[column]][is.nan(extracted[[column]])] <- NA_real_
		buffer.env[original.i, column] <- extracted[[column]]
	}
	
}
```

Both methods ignore missing cell values. Fully outside or all-missing areas receive `NA` estimates and zero coverage. A target without usable geometry retains its ID with `NA` estimates and `NA` coverage. These conventions apply to all three area sections.

Population SD describes spatial heterogeneity within an area. It does not measure uncertainty in the interpolated surface or its mean. A proper estimation of uncertainty needs information about measurement or model error; raster cells should not automatically be treated as independent observations for a standard error.

## Check the buffer results

The methods should agree on means and coverage. `buffer.env` also contains medians, SDs and counts, and retains one row per original tree/stem record.

```{r}
#| label: check-buffer-results

comparison.columns <- setdiff(names(buffer.terra), names(targets))

stopifnot(identical(buffer.env$point_id, targets$point_id),
          isTRUE(all.equal(buffer.terra[comparison.columns],
                           buffer.env[comparison.columns], tolerance = 1e-5)))

head(buffer.env[c("point_id", "Mnemonic", "mean.soil_P_mgkg", "median.soil_P_mgkg",
                  "stdev.soil_P_mgkg", "coverage.soil_P_mgkg")])
```

# Extract from quadrats

## Construct quadrats at two resolutions

Reuse `make_quadrats_fast()` and the standard table with `quadrat_id`, `xmin`, `ymin`, `xmax` and `ymax`. The polygons come directly from those bounds. `grid_id` distinguishes IDs that repeat between resolutions; these IDs are separate from the census `Quadrat` naming convention.

```{r}
#| label: quadrat-polygons

q20 <- make_quadrats_fast(0, 0, 1000, 500, 20, 20)
q50 <- make_quadrats_fast(0, 0, 1000, 500, 50, 50)
q20$grid_id <- "20m"
q50$grid_id <- "50m"
quadrat.table <- rbind(q20, q50)

geometry <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(quadrat.table)), function(i)
{
	q <- quadrat.table[i, ]
	corners <- cbind(c(q$xmin, q$xmax, q$xmax, q$xmin, q$xmin),
	                 c(q$ymin, q$ymin, q$ymax, q$ymax, q$ymin))
	st_polygon(list(corners))
})

quadrats <- st_sf(quadrat.table, geometry = st_sfc(geometry, crs = st_crs(crs(terrain))))
quadrat.i <- which(!st_is_empty(quadrats))
quadrat.area <- as.numeric(st_area(quadrats))
quadrat.key <- paste(quadrat.table$grid_id, quadrat.table$quadrat_id, sep = "/")
stopifnot(nrow(q20) == 1250L, nrow(q50) == 200L, !anyDuplicated(quadrat.key))
```

## Extract environmental summaries

Both resolutions use the same environmental layers and weighting as the buffers. No raster needs to be resampled to the quadrat size.

### Method 1 with terra::extract()

```{r}
#| label: terra-quadrat-means

quadrat.terra <- quadrat.table
for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		quadrat.terra[[paste0("mean.", variable)]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(quadrat.table))
		quadrat.terra[[paste0("coverage.", variable)]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(quadrat.table))
	}
	if(!length(quadrat.i)) next
	means <- terra::extract(layers, vect(quadrats[quadrat.i, ]), exact = TRUE, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
	counts <- terra::extract(!is.na(layers), vect(quadrats[quadrat.i, ]), exact = TRUE, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)
	i <- match(seq_along(quadrat.i), means$ID)
	j <- match(seq_along(quadrat.i), counts$ID)

	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		value <- means[[variable]][i]
		value[is.nan(value)] <- NA_real_
		coverage <- counts[[variable]][j] * prod(res(layers)) / quadrat.area[quadrat.i]
		coverage[is.na(coverage)] <- 0
		quadrat.terra[quadrat.i, paste0("mean.", variable)] <- value
		quadrat.terra[quadrat.i, paste0("coverage.", variable)] <- pmin(1, pmax(0, coverage))
	}
}
```

### Method 2 with exactextractr::exact_extract()

Keep both `grid_id` and `quadrat_id` when matching results, since a quadrat ID alone is not unique across grids.

```{r}
#| label: exactextractr-quadrat-summaries

quadrat.env <- quadrat.table
for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		for(statistic in c("mean", "median", "stdev", "count", "coverage"))
			quadrat.env[[paste(statistic, variable, sep = ".")]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(quadrat.table))
	}
	if(!length(quadrat.i)) next
	extracted <- exact_extract(layers, quadrats[quadrat.i, ],
		fun = c("mean", "median", "stdev", "count"),
		append_cols = c("grid_id", "quadrat_id"), full_colnames = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		coverage <- extracted[[paste0("count.", variable)]] * prod(res(layers)) / quadrat.area[quadrat.i]
		coverage[is.na(coverage)] <- 0
		extracted[[paste0("coverage.", variable)]] <- pmin(1, pmax(0, coverage))
	}
	extracted.key <- paste(extracted$grid_id, extracted$quadrat_id, sep = "/")
	original.i <- match(extracted.key, quadrat.key)
	for(column in setdiff(names(extracted), c("grid_id", "quadrat_id")))
	{
		extracted[[column]][is.nan(extracted[[column]])] <- NA_real_
		quadrat.env[original.i, column] <- extracted[[column]]
	}
}
```

## Check the quadrat results

The output retains the bounds and identifiers for both resolutions, with one row per supplied quadrat.

```{r}
#| label: check-quadrat-results

comparison.columns <- setdiff(names(quadrat.terra), names(quadrat.table))
stopifnot(identical(quadrat.env[c("grid_id", "quadrat_id")],
                    quadrat.table[c("grid_id", "quadrat_id")]),
          isTRUE(all.equal(quadrat.terra[comparison.columns],
                           quadrat.env[comparison.columns], tolerance = 1e-5)))
table(quadrat.env$grid_id)
head(quadrat.env[c("grid_id", "quadrat_id", "mean.soil_P_mgkg", "coverage.soil_P_mgkg")])
```

# Extract from arbitrary polygons

## Construct the polygons

One polygon lies inside the plot; the other crosses its western boundary. Existing `sf` polygons or multipolygons in the same local plot frame can enter here. Invalid shapes need correction before extraction. An empty geometry represents a target whose location remains unresolved and keeps an `NA` output row.

```{r}
#| label: irregular-polygons

regions <- st_sf(polygon_id = c("interior", "western_edge"),
	geometry = st_sfc(
		st_polygon(list(cbind(c(100, 240, 190, 100), c(150, 150, 280, 150)))),
		st_polygon(list(cbind(c(-15, 60, 60, -15, -15), c(30, 30, 80, 100, 30)))),
		crs = st_crs(crs(terrain))
	))
polygon.table <- st_drop_geometry(regions)
polygon.i <- which(!st_is_empty(regions))
polygon.area <- as.numeric(st_area(regions))
stopifnot(!anyNA(regions$polygon_id), !anyDuplicated(regions$polygon_id),
          all(st_is_valid(regions)), all(is.finite(polygon.area[polygon.i])),
          all(polygon.area[polygon.i] > 0))
```

## Extract environmental summaries

Only the target geometry and its ID have changed. Coverage still uses the full polygon area, including any part outside the raster.

### Method 1 with terra::extract()

```{r}
#| label: terra-polygon-means

polygon.terra <- polygon.table
for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		polygon.terra[[paste0("mean.", variable)]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(polygon.table))
		polygon.terra[[paste0("coverage.", variable)]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(polygon.table))
	}
	if(!length(polygon.i)) next
	means <- terra::extract(layers, vect(regions[polygon.i, ]), exact = TRUE, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
	counts <- terra::extract(!is.na(layers), vect(regions[polygon.i, ]), exact = TRUE, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)
	i <- match(seq_along(polygon.i), means$ID)
	j <- match(seq_along(polygon.i), counts$ID)

	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		value <- means[[variable]][i]
		value[is.nan(value)] <- NA_real_
		coverage <- counts[[variable]][j] * prod(res(layers)) / polygon.area[polygon.i]
		coverage[is.na(coverage)] <- 0
		polygon.terra[polygon.i, paste0("mean.", variable)] <- value
		polygon.terra[polygon.i, paste0("coverage.", variable)] <- pmin(1, pmax(0, coverage))
	}
}
```

### Method 2 with exactextractr::exact_extract()

```{r}
#| label: exactextractr-polygon-summaries

polygon.env <- polygon.table
for(source in names(environment))
{
	layers <- environment[[source]]
	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		for(statistic in c("mean", "median", "stdev", "count", "coverage"))
			polygon.env[[paste(statistic, variable, sep = ".")]] <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(polygon.table))
	}
	if(!length(polygon.i)) next
	extracted <- exact_extract(layers, regions[polygon.i, ],
		fun = c("mean", "median", "stdev", "count"),
		append_cols = "polygon_id", full_colnames = TRUE, progress = FALSE)

	for(variable in names(layers))
	{
		coverage <- extracted[[paste0("count.", variable)]] * prod(res(layers)) / polygon.area[polygon.i]
		coverage[is.na(coverage)] <- 0
		extracted[[paste0("coverage.", variable)]] <- pmin(1, pmax(0, coverage))
	}
	original.i <- match(extracted$polygon_id, regions$polygon_id)
	for(column in setdiff(names(extracted), "polygon_id"))
	{
		extracted[[column]][is.nan(extracted[[column]])] <- NA_real_
		polygon.env[original.i, column] <- extracted[[column]]
	}
}
```

## Check the polygon results

The western-edge polygon demonstrates partial coverage. Missing soil cells can reduce valid coverage further, independently of elevation coverage.

```{r}
#| label: check-polygon-results

comparison.columns <- setdiff(names(polygon.terra), names(polygon.table))
stopifnot(identical(polygon.env$polygon_id, regions$polygon_id),
          isTRUE(all.equal(polygon.terra[comparison.columns],
                           polygon.env[comparison.columns], tolerance = 1e-5)))
polygon.env[c("polygon_id", "mean.elevation_m", "coverage.elevation_m",
              "mean.soil_P_mgkg", "coverage.soil_P_mgkg")]
```

# Save results and reuse them

Save native raster groups separately to retain their original resolution. GeoTIFF files can be loaded directly with `rast()` in later work. The common-grid object can be saved as an additional explicit product if needed. Tabular outputs remain separate from geometry and can feed later habitat analyses or mapping workflows.

```{r}
#| label: save-environment
#| results: hide

writeRaster(terrain, file.path(output.dir, "bci-terrain.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
writeRaster(soil, file.path(output.dir, "bci-soil.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
write.csv(point.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-point-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(buffer.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-buffer-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(quadrat.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-quadrat-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(polygon.env, file.path(output.dir, "bci-polygon-environment.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Independent raster inputs in a later session.
saved.soil <- rast(file.path(output.dir, "bci-soil.tif"))
stopifnot(compareGeom(saved.soil, soil))
```

Keep the original inputs, source licences, parameter choices and executed code with the analysis. The examples above use the same target rows for each variable, while the valid observations contributing to each summary can differ. Any subsequent complete-case filtering or coverage threshold should be explicit in that analysis.

# Software references and versions

-   [terra extraction](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/extract.html) and [point interpolation](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/interpIDW.html).
-   [terra grid comparisons](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/compareGeom.html), [aggregation](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/aggregate.html) and [resampling](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/resample.html).
-   [exactextractr summaries and custom functions](https://isciences.gitlab.io/exactextractr/reference/exact_extract.html).
-   [sf coordinate transformations](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/st_transform.html).

```{r}
#| label: environment-session

packages <- c("terra", "sf", "interp", "exactextractr")
data.frame(software = c("R", packages),
           version = c(as.character(getRversion()),
                       sapply(packages, function(x) as.character(packageVersion(x)))))
# sessionInfo() gives a full session record for an analysis archive.
```
